record.paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Connexive Logic
record.original_question: Develop a model-theoretic account of negation as cancellation in which the cancelling effect of negation does not depend mainly on how semantic consequence is defined, and then determine whether that framework validates the characteristic theses of connexive logic for a wide range of truth conditions for the conditional.

evidence.quote: Open problem 5 How can we model the negation as cancellation model-theoretically so that the cancellation feature does not depend too much on the definition of the semantic consequence relation? Moreover, once we have a model-theoretic framework, do the characteristic theses of connexive logic get included for a wide range of truth conditions for the conditional?

However, is Priest’s approach satisfactory as a formalization of the idea of negation as cancellation? In particular, the approach seems to be dependent too much on the definition of the semantic consequence relation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. In connexive logic, negation is sometimes understood according to the "cancellation" conception: asserting both A and ¬A produces mutual annihilation, so a contradiction conveys no content. The characteristic theses of connexive logic are:
  • Aristotle's theses:  ¬(¬A → A)  and  ¬(A → ¬A);
  • Boethius' theses:  (A → B) → ¬(A → ¬B)  and  (A → ¬B) → ¬(A → B);
together with the requirement that the conditional → be non-symmetric, i.e. (A → B) → (B → A) is not valid.

Existing formalizations of negation-as-cancellation (e.g. Priest's approach) build the cancellation effect into the definition of the semantic consequence relation ⊨ rather than into the truth conditions of the connectives in a model.

Problem. Construct a model-theoretic semantics ⟨M, ⊨⟩ for a propositional language with connectives {¬, →, ∧, ∨} that realizes negation-as-cancellation in the following sense:

(i) The cancelling/neutralizing effect of ¬ is encoded in the structure of models M (e.g. in the valuation clauses for ¬ and for the other connectives), and not principally in the definition of the consequence relation Γ ⊨ A.

(ii) Under the resulting semantics, the logic determined by ⊨ should validate Aristotle's theses and Boethius' theses, and should fail to validate (A → B) → (B → A), thereby qualifying as a connexive logic.

(iii) The framework should accommodate a wide class of admissible truth conditions for the conditional →: determine, as explicitly as possible, the family of conditional truth-clauses (for instance, variably strict, relevant, intuitionistic-style, or possible-worlds based clauses) for which the connexive theses in (ii) remain valid in the constructed semantics.

Deliverables. Provide such a semantic framework, prove that it makes the characteristic connexive theses valid, characterize the range of conditional truth conditions over which validity is preserved, and exhibit a soundness (and, if possible, completeness) result for an associated proof system.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is listed among ten open problems in connexive logic in a recent (2025) volume "60 Years of Connexive Logic". The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on connexive logic and recent surveys describe model-theoretic accounts of negation-as-cancellation as an unresolved challenge, with existing approaches (notably Priest's) criticized for embedding the cancellation effect in the consequence relation rather than the model theory. No published solution providing a fully model-theoretic framework with the desired generality was found.

status_evidence.title: Ten Open Problems in Connexive Logic (Springer chapter)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists ten open problems in connexive logic, including the model-theoretic formalization of negation as cancellation.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly listed as open.

status_evidence.title: Connexive Logic (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses the cancellation view of negation and notes difficulties in providing semantics where cancellation is not enforced via the consequence relation.
status_evidence.claim: Existing model-theoretic accounts of cancellation negation are widely regarded as unsatisfactory.

status_evidence.title: Negation as Cancellation, Connexive Logic, and qLPm (Wansing & Priest discussion)
status_evidence.snippet: Examines Priest's qLPm formalization of cancellation, where the cancellation feature is tied to the definition of semantic consequence.
status_evidence.claim: Current formalizations build cancellation into the consequence relation, motivating the open problem.
